reconcile.connective: Defenders distinguish the two targets: the resident stranger (ger) who has come under Israel's God is loved, while the Canaanite nations face herem as judicial punishment for incorrigible wickedness.

discrepancy.connective: Thomas Paine pressed the moral incompatibility directly, holding that the divine command to exterminate the Canaanites — "even to suckling infants" — reads as the word of a demon, not of the God who elsewhere enjoins kindness to the stranger.

skeptic.name: Thomas Paine
skeptic.attribution: Thomas Paine (d. 1809), The Age of Reason (1794-1807)

excerpts.excerpt_text: This relentless doom of extermination which God denounced against those tribes of Canaan cannot be reconciled with the attributes of the divine character, except on the assumption that their gross idolatry and enormous wickedness left no reasonable hope of their repentance and amendment.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: JFB names the exact tension (the extermination command vs. God's character, which elsewhere commands loving the stranger) and supplies the standard harmonization: the Canaanites are exempted from mercy as incorrigible idolaters under judicial sentence, not as ordinary outsiders.

pd_work.resource: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown, Commentary Critical and Explanatory on the Whole Bible (1871), on Deuteronomy 7:2
pd_work.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
pd_work.note: JFB engages this passage directly, arguing the extermination doom is consistent with the divine character only as judicial punishment of incorrigible idolatry — the harmonizing reading keyed to this contradiction.
